items.title: sprintf()/pack()/bin2hex() _exit(137) at hard memory limit where 8.5.11 raised a catchable OOM (incomplete fallible-alloc conversion, 8.5.12/8.4.27)
items.body:
### Description

Since commit `31c0ea7d` ("Avoid state corruption via bailout", CVE-2026-109618/109619), a **non-fallible** allocation that would cross the new hard memory limit (default 200% of `memory_limit`) terminates the process via `_exit(137)` in `zend_mm_hard_limit_error()` (`Zend/zend_alloc.c`). Most allocation sites were moved to the new fallible API, but several core functions still allocate non-fallibly from a small, caller-supplied size, so they kill the whole process instead of raising the catchable "Allowed memory size exhausted" fatal that 8.5.11 produced for the same input.

The following code:

```php
<?php
sprintf("%400000000s", "");
```

Run with: `php -n -d memory_limit=128M repro.php`

Resulted in this output (8.5.12):

```
Hard memory limit of 268435456 bytes exhausted (tried to allocate 505413632 bytes) in Command line code on line 1
```
Exit code **137** — process terminated; the allocation is never actually performed (the hard-limit check rejects first).

But I expected this output instead (the 8.5.11 behavior):

```
Fatal error: Allowed memory size of 134217728 bytes exhausted (tried to allocate 503316512 bytes) in Command line code on line 1
```
Exit code **255** — catchable fatal, the process/worker survives.

The same process kill occurs from other small integer parameters — `pack("x300000000")`, `number_format(1.0, 100000000)`, `bcadd("1","1",100000000)` — and from large in-heap inputs to `bin2hex` / `base64_encode` / `urlencode` / `var_export` / `convert_uuencode` / `utf8_encode` / `quoted_printable_encode`. A crafted `phar://` manifest length triggers it from a ~100-byte file.

Sites still using the non-fallible allocator in 8.5.12:
- `smart_string_alloc()` in `PAD_CHAR` — `main/spprintf.c`
- `zend_string_alloc(outputsize, 0)` — `ext/standard/pack.c:431`
- `zend_string_safe_alloc(..., 0)` in `php_bin2hex()` / `php_utf8_encode()` — `ext/standard/string.c`

Mechanism: `zend_mm_check_limit()` calls `zend_mm_hard_limit_error()` → `_exit(137)` when `!heap->fallible` and the allocation would cross `hard_limit`. Routing these sites through the fallible API (`femalloc` / `zend_string_finit` / `smart_str_ferealloc`) would keep the OOM catchable, consistent with the rest of the patch.

Reproduces identically on 8.4.27 (8.4.26 behaves like 8.5.11). The path is in `Zend/zend_alloc.c`, so it is platform-independent; tested here on official Windows x64 NTS builds.

### PHP Version

```plain
PHP 8.5.12 (cli) (built: Oct 20 2026 04:19:56) (NTS Visual C++ 2022 x64)
Copyright (c) The PHP Group
Built by The PHP Group
Zend Engine v4.5.12, Copyright (c) Zend Technologies
```

### Operating System

Windows 11 (code path is OS-independent — Zend/zend_alloc.c)

items.title: Allocation-failure call sites still on zend_error_noreturn(E_ERROR) on master (zend_strtod.c "Balloc() failed", zend_multiply.h) — the EOL-7.4 minimal mitigation hardened these, master did not
items.body:
## Context

While studying the fixes for GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w / GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp (thank you for the
delayed-OOM machinery in 3584a98bda — the design is excellent), we noticed a consistency
gap between the two fix branches:

- The EOL-7.4 minimal mitigation **712e60f9ed** converted several allocation-failure call
  sites to the fail-fast `zend_mm_safe_error_ex()` path.
- The full 8.x fix and current **master** kept several such call sites on
  `zend_error_noreturn(E_ERROR, ...)`, i.e. they still run the error machinery and bail
  out via longjmp from the failing context — the exact pattern the advisory describes as
  dangerous when the allocator is in a failing state.

This is an **informational hardening-consistency observation, not a vulnerability report** —
see the empirical section: we could not reach any of these paths from PHP userland under
the conditions we tested.

## Call sites in question (master, checked 2026-10-22)

| Location | Code | Note |
|---|---|---|
| `Zend/zend_strtod.c` ~590 / ~603 | `zend_error_noreturn(E_ERROR, "Balloc() failed to allocate memory")` when `MALLOC()` (raw `malloc`, `#define MALLOC malloc` at ~237) returns NULL | dtoa allocates Bigints outside Zend MM entirely (also unaccounted by `memory_limit`) |
| `Zend/zend_multiply.h` ~343 / ~355 | `zend_error_noreturn(E_ERROR, "Possible integer overflow ...")` | size-arithmetic checks; 7.4 converted both |
| `ext/sodium/libsodium.c` ~42 | `zend_error_noreturn(E_ERROR, "Memory allocation too large ...")` | untouched in both branches |

## Empirical work (why we rate this informational, not exploitable)

We tried hard to reach the `Balloc()` path from userland before writing this up.
PHP 8.4.27, arm64 (docker), instrumentation at three levels — all evidence below is
reproducible and we are happy to share the tooling (a ~30-line `LD_PRELOAD` malloc
interposer, RLIMIT_AS sweep harness, phase-marker snippets):

1. **Phase markers** (STDERR markers around string-build vs conversion): across an
   RLIMIT_AS sweep at **1 KB granularity**, every allocation failure occurred during
   string *construction* (Zend MM chunk mmap), before `zend_strtod` was ever entered.
   `FAIL_IN_CONVERSION` count: **0**. The transition was a cliff, not a window
   (67247 KB → fail in build, 67248 KB → full success).
2. **strace** (mmap/brk/mremap bracketed by the same markers): **0** memory-mapping
   syscalls during the conversion phase, both with comfortable VA and at the boundary.
3. **LD_PRELOAD malloc interposer** (libc-call level, which strace cannot see):
   conversion performs a **constant 11 malloc calls / 428 requested bytes** regardless of
   a **1024× input-length difference** (4,096 vs 4,194,304 mantissa digits). Controls:
   marker-only run = 0 allocations; a low-level `fwrite()` marker variant reproduced the
   same 11/428B figure, ruling out instrumentation overhead. Preliminary return-address
   attribution places one call near `zend_strtod+0xee4`.

In other words: for the tested input domain, dtoa's memory need is bounded (digit
truncation before Bigint construction; freelist/private pool absorbs the rest), so
RLIMIT_AS pressure always surfaces in the string BUILD phase, where the new
delayed-OOM machinery handles it gracefully. We did **not** find a way to make the
libc allocator fail *inside* the conversion.

## Questions

1. Is leaving these on `zend_error_noreturn` intentional — i.e. does the delayed-OOM
   layer on master also cover a libc-malloc failure deep inside dtoa, making the 7.4-style
   conversion unnecessary there?
2. If it is an oversight, would a small PR converting the four call sites above to the
   fail-fast pattern (mirroring 712e60f9ed) be welcome? Happy to send it.
3. Separately: is the fact that dtoa allocates via raw `malloc()` (outside `memory_limit`
   accounting) considered acceptable? Our measurements suggest per-conversion usage is
   tiny and bounded, so this may be fine as-is — asking for completeness.

## Reproduction context

The interest in this area came from lab work on the php2shell chains (public PoC and a
public Metasploit module PR exist for CVE-2026-109618/109619). We validated the patched
build behavior end-to-end: on 8.4.27 the public chain dies at the heap-leak stage with
zero worker crashes, consistent with the fix cutting off stale-state reuse. No new
exploitation is reported or implied by this issue.

items.title: var_destroy() UAF also reachable through SplObjectStorage::__unserialize() — separate entry point from #24481
DateTime::setTime() in the repeated hour of Europe/Dublin moves to the later occurrence (an hour ahead)
items.body:
### Description

On the day clocks go back, `DateTime::setTime()` on a time in the repeated hour in `Europe/Dublin` moves it to the *second* occurrence of the wall time, an hour later, even when the new time is only seconds away on the same wall clock. Europe/London, at the same instant and with the same UTC offsets, keeps the first occurrence.

The following code:

```php
<?php
foreach (['Europe/Dublin', 'Europe/London', 'Europe/Amsterdam'] as $tz) {
    $d = (new DateTimeImmutable('2026-10-25 00:10:30 UTC'))->setTimezone(new DateTimeZone($tz));
    $e = $d->setTime((int) $d->format('H'), 10, 59);
    printf("%-16s %s -> %s (%+ds)\n", $tz, $d->format('Y-m-d H:i:s T'), $e->format('H:i:s T'), $e->getTimestamp() - $d->getTimestamp());
}
```

Resulted in this output:

```
Europe/Dublin    2026-10-25 01:10:30 IST -> 01:10:59 GMT (+3629s)
Europe/London    2026-10-25 01:10:30 BST -> 01:10:59 BST (+29s)
Europe/Amsterdam 2026-10-25 02:10:30 CEST -> 02:10:59 CEST (+29s)
```

But I expected this output instead:

```
Europe/Dublin    2026-10-25 01:10:30 IST -> 01:10:59 IST (+29s)
Europe/London    2026-10-25 01:10:30 BST -> 01:10:59 BST (+29s)
Europe/Amsterdam 2026-10-25 02:10:30 CEST -> 02:10:59 CEST (+29s)
```

Dublin and London both switch from UTC+1 to UTC+0 at 01:00 UTC on 25 October 2026, so I'd expect them to behave the same. The difference seems to be that the tz database models Irish time with a negative DST offset: IST (UTC+1) is the standard time and GMT is flagged as DST. So keeping or choosing a DST state when resolving the ambiguous wall time gives the opposite result to every other zone.

Anything that rounds a time with `setTime()`, `modify('...')` or date libraries built on them (e.g. Carbon's `endOfMinute()`) is affected. We hit it in production: Laravel's scheduler computed "end of the current minute" this way, so during that hour each run waited an hour instead of seconds. That bug is being fixed on the Laravel side (https://github.com/laravel/framework/pull/62197), but the root cause looks like it's here.

### PHP Version

```
PHP 8.5.12 (cli) (built: Oct 19 2026 17:02:46) (ZTS)
timezone_version_get(): 2026.5
```

### Operating System

macOS, and Debian GNU/Linux 13 (trixie) with PHP 8.5.12 NTS

items.title: JIT: function with >~1.7 MB of machine code corrupts JIT buffer accounting; next compilation crashes (SIGBUS on arm64)
items.body:
### Description

With function JIT (`opcache.jit=function`, also `1204`), compiling a single function whose
generated machine code exceeds roughly 1.7 MB makes `opcache_get_status()['jit']['buffer_free']`
**increase** by about the size of that code, instead of decreasing. The next compilation that
emits code then crashes the process with SIGBUS (exit status 138).

The following code:

```php
<?php
// php -d opcache.enable_cli=1 -d opcache.jit=function -d opcache.jit_buffer_size=64M \
//     -d opcache.file_update_protection=0 -d memory_limit=1G repro.php

$body = '';
for ($k = 0; $k < 3000; $k++) {
    $body .= "    \$r[" . ($k % 32) . "] = \$v + $k;\n";
}
file_put_contents(__DIR__ . '/big.php', "<?php\nfunction big(array &\$r, int \$v) {\n$body}\n");
file_put_contents(__DIR__ . '/next.php', "<?php\necho \"next file compiled\\n\";\n");

$free = fn() => opcache_get_status(false)['jit']['buffer_free'];
$before = $free();
include __DIR__ . '/big.php';
printf("JIT buffer_free changed by %+d bytes (should be negative: code was added)\n", $free() - $before);
include __DIR__ . '/next.php';
echo "survived\n";
```

Resulted in this output:

```
JIT buffer_free changed by +1859668 bytes (should be negative: code was added)
Bus error: 10      (exit status 138)
```

But I expected this output instead:

```
JIT buffer_free changed by -1859668 bytes (should be negative: code was added)
next file compiled
survived
```

### Observations

- The threshold is the size of one function's machine code, not the input: with this shape,
  2850 statements add 1,766,964 bytes and work; 2851 statements report `buffer_free` going
  *up* by 1,767,384 and the next compilation crashes. Closures and named functions, by-value
  and by-reference array parameters all behave the same.
- The big function itself can be called fine afterwards; it's the *next* compilation that
  faults, which fits the buffer's free pointer having moved backwards.
- Reproduces with `opcache.jit=function` and `1204` and JIT buffer sizes of 16M, 64M and 128M.
  Doesn't with `1201` (optimization level 1), `1215` (compile on first call, since `big()`
  isn't called here), tracing (nothing compiled at load), or a 1M buffer (presumably it doesn't
  fit at all).
- `opcache.file_update_protection=0` is only there so the freshly written files are cached
  and JIT-compiled; with pre-existing files the flag isn't needed.
- Found in a PHP emulator that generates large PHP functions at run time; it showed up there as
  "zend_mm_heap corrupted", "Undefined array key" on impossible lines, and bus errors.

### PHP Version

```
PHP 8.5.12 (cli) (built: Oct 19 2026 17:02:46) (NTS)   [Homebrew]
```

### Operating System

macOS (Darwin 27.0.0), Apple M1 (arm64)

items.title: FPM: pools with different disable_functions sharing one opcache run scripts wrongly (var_export() calls var_dump(), SIGSEGV in the restricted pool) on 8.4/8.5/8.6
items.body:
### Description

*Quoted text written with an LLM and checked by a human developer.*

> Two pools in **one** FPM master, one with `php_admin_value[disable_functions]` and one without, share the opcache. Once a script has been compiled and cached through one pool, the other pool executes it wrongly: an internal function call is dispatched to a different internal function, and a worker of the restricted pool can crash.

`fpm.conf`:

```ini
[global]
daemonize = no
error_log = /dev/stderr
[a]
user = nobody
listen = /tmp/a.sock
listen.owner = nobody
pm = static
pm.max_children = 1
php_admin_value[disable_functions] = exec
[b]
user = nobody
listen = /tmp/b.sock
listen.owner = nobody
pm = static
pm.max_children = 1
```

`t.php`:

```php
<?php
echo var_export([1, 'x' => true], true), "\n";
```

> Request `t.php` through pool `a`, then through pool `b` (a ~20-line FastCGI client, `fcgi.php`, is attached below so that no web server is needed). Resulting output, `php:8.5-fpm` (8.5.12), default settings (opcache is built in):

```
pool a: array (
  0 => 1,
  'x' => true,
)
pool b: array(2) {
  [0]=>
  int(1)
  ["x"]=>
  bool(true)
}
bool(true)
```

> Pool `b` printed the output of `var_dump()` (and its return value) instead of `var_export()`. Expected output: the same text as pool `a`. With the order reversed (`b` first, then `a`) pool `a`, the one with `exec` disabled, prints `debug_zval_dump()` style output (`array(2) interned {...}`).

> On Ubuntu's 8.5.4 (`8.5.4-0ubuntu1.5`, `-n` with `zend_extension=opcache`) pool `b` fails with `convert_uudecode() expects exactly 1 argument, 2 given` for the same script, i.e. the call is dispatched to a third function.

> A script that calls the disabled function itself (`t2.php`: `echo exec('echo hi');`), requested through `b` first and then through `a`, kills the worker of the restricted pool:

```
WARNING: [pool a] child 10 exited on signal 11 (SIGSEGV) after 2.015193 seconds from start
```

> What I checked:
>
> | | result |
> | -- | -- |
> | 8.5.12, 8.4.27 (official `php:*-fpm` images), 8.6.0RC4 (`php:8.6-rc-fpm`, ZTS), Ubuntu 8.5.4 | wrong function called |
> | 8.3.36 (`php:8.3-fpm`) | correct |
> | `opcache.enable=0` | correct |
> | `opcache.optimization_level=0` | correct |
> | 8.4 without `zend_extension=opcache` (`-n`) | correct |
> | default `opcache.optimization_level` with the bit `0x20` or the bit `0x40` cleared (one at a time; every other bit alone makes no difference) | correct |
> | two separate FPM masters, one pool each, same `disable_functions` split (8.5.12 and 8.4.27) | correct, no cross-effect |

> I did not trace what exactly gets cached or resolved by index or by pointer, so I cannot say more than that the optimizer passes `0x20` (DFA) and `0x40` (call graph) are both needed. I saw no case where a disabled function actually ran: the restricted pool crashed or printed the output of another function, but never executed `exec`. FPM accepts `php_admin_value[disable_functions]` per pool, so a setup like this is not exotic, and the symptom (wrong output rather than an error) is hard to diagnose; the workaround is `opcache.enable=0`, or one master per differing `disable_functions` set.

> ~~I found no open or closed report about this.~~ Same root cause as GH-17733. Related but different: #21974 (SIGSEGV with `disable_functions` per pool, ZTS builds only) and #24047 (system id and frameless functions).

> To reproduce (podman/docker; the directory holds `fpm.conf`, `t.php`, `t2.php`, `fcgi.php`, `run.sh`):

```sh
docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/m docker.io/library/php:8.5-fpm sh /m/run.sh "a b a b" t.php
docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/m docker.io/library/php:8.5-fpm sh /m/run.sh "b a" t2.php
docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/m docker.io/library/php:8.5-fpm sh /m/run.sh "a b a b" t.php -d opcache.enable=0   # correct
```

<details><summary>control: one master per pool (correct on 8.5.12 and 8.4.27)</summary>

```sh
sed -n '1,10p' /m/fpm.conf > /tmp/fpm-a.conf
{ sed -n '1,3p' /m/fpm.conf; sed -n '11,16p' /m/fpm.conf; } > /tmp/fpm-b.conf
php-fpm -y /tmp/fpm-a.conf -F >/m/fpm-a.out 2>&1 &
php-fpm -y /tmp/fpm-b.conf -F >/m/fpm-b.out 2>&1 &
sleep 2
for p in a b a b b a; do printf -- "pool %s: " "$p"; php /m/fcgi.php /tmp/$p.sock /m/t.php 2>&1 | tr '\n' ' '; echo; done
```

</details>

`fcgi.php`:

```php
<?php
// Minimal FastCGI GET client: php fcgi.php /tmp/a.sock /m/t.php
[$sock, $script] = [$argv[1], $argv[2]];
$rec = fn(int $t, string $b) => pack('CCnnCx', 1, $t, 1, strlen($b), 0) . $b;
$kv = function (string $k, string $v): string {
    $l = fn(int $n) => $n < 128 ? chr($n) : pack('N', $n | 0x80000000);
    return $l(strlen($k)) . $l(strlen($v)) . $k . $v;
};
$p = $kv('SCRIPT_FILENAME', $script) . $kv('REQUEST_METHOD', 'GET') . $kv('SCRIPT_NAME', '/t.php')
   . $kv('SERVER_PROTOCOL', 'HTTP/1.1') . $kv('REQUEST_URI', '/t.php') . $kv('QUERY_STRING', '');
$s = stream_socket_client("unix://$sock", $en, $es, 10);
fwrite($s, $rec(1, pack('nCx5', 1, 0)) . $rec(4, $p) . $rec(4, '') . $rec(5, ''));
$out = '';
while (!feof($s)) {
    $h = stream_get_contents($s, 8);
    if (strlen($h) < 8) break;
    $d = unpack('Cv/Ct/nid/nlen/Cpad', $h);
    $body = $d['len'] + $d['pad'] ? stream_get_contents($s, $d['len'] + $d['pad']) : '';
    if ($d['t'] === 6 || $d['t'] === 7) $out .= substr($body, 0, $d['len']);
    if ($d['t'] === 3) break;
}
echo preg_replace('~^.*?\r\n\r\n~s', '', $out) ?: "(empty response / connection reset)\n";
```

`run.sh`:

```sh
ord=$1; scr=$2; shift 2
php -v | head -1
php-fpm "$@" -y /m/fpm.conf -F >/m/fpm.out 2>&1 &
sleep 2
for p in $ord; do printf -- "pool %s: " "$p"; php /m/fcgi.php /tmp/$p.sock /m/$scr 2>&1 | tr '\n' ' '; echo; done
grep -E "SIGSEGV|signal" /m/fpm.out
```

### PHP Version

```
PHP 8.5.12 (cli) (built: Oct 21 2026 15:49:51) (NTS)   [php:8.5-fpm]
PHP 8.4.27 (cli) (built: Oct 21 2026 15:53:31) (NTS)   [php:8.4-fpm, opcache loaded]
PHP 8.6.0RC4 (cli) (built: Oct 21 2026 22:05:36) (ZTS) [php:8.6-rc-fpm]
PHP 8.5.4-0ubuntu1.5 (Ubuntu 26.04)
```

### Operating System

Debian (official Docker images), Ubuntu 26.04
